summary: Addresses the key management side of the TCP MD5 Signature Option, used mostly by BGP. Its security depends heavily on the quality of the keys used to compute the signature, so the document discusses the requirements for that keying material. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A signature on a message is only as good as the secret behind it. This memo gives advice on picking and handling the secrets used to sign certain router conversations.

questions: how long should a tcp md5 key be
how often should bgp md5 keys change
what is tcp md5 signature option
subtitle: How long, how private and how fresh the secret keys behind BGP's TCP MD5 signatures should be.

tldr.problem: The TCP MD5 Signature Option protects BGP sessions, but its security depends mostly on the secret key. Short, shared, long-lived keys are easy to guess.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC estimates how fast an attacker could guess keys and concludes that keys should be 12 to 24 bytes, not shared across peerings, and changed at least every 90 days.
tldr.outcome: It gives operators and implementers concrete key guidance, but it is an Informational memo and creates no new protocol.

facts.label: Minimum entropy
facts.value: About 68 bits, rounded up to 80 bits

facts.label: Key sharing
facts.value: Not shared among multiple BGP peerings

today: RFC 3562 is an Informational RFC from July 2003. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata, and it gives guidance rather than a protocol.

sections.title: Why the Key Matters
sections.content:
The TCP MD5 Signature Option from RFC 2385 is used mostly by BGP and has been widely deployed in critical parts of Internet infrastructure. RFC 3562 points out that the strength of the scheme depends heavily on the keying material used to compute the MD5 signature.

Theoretical attacks on the simple MAC construction in RFC 2385 exist, but they need so many text and MAC pairs that the author considers key-guessing the main threat. The RFC therefore takes a quantitative approach to how strong keys need to be.

Summary of the advice: keys SHOULD be between 12 and 24 bytes, SHOULD NOT be shared among several BGP peering arrangements, and SHOULD be changed at least every 90 days.
sections.plainLanguage: A secret handshake only works if the secret is hard to guess. This memo is about making the secret hard to guess.

sections.title: How Fast Can an Attacker Guess?
sections.content:
To size the key, the RFC estimates attacker speed. It starts from an MD5 performance study in RFC 1810 (87 Mbits/second in software) and assumes Moore's Law to project about 2.1 Gbits/second for around 2002. An attacker would target short packets, such as a bare ACK of about 40 bytes. MD5 works on 64-byte blocks, so this gives roughly 4.1e6 single-block MD5 operations per second on one CPU.

A single CPU is the optimistic case for the defender. The RFC notes that the Code Red worm infected over 350,000 hosts in its first 14 hours, and a stealthy worm might reach 1 million hosts or more. That would raise the rate to between 1.0e11 and 1.0e13 MD5 operations per second.

For hardware, the RFC recalls the 1997 machine built for about USD$250,000 that could find a DES key in under 1 week. It assumes a similar approach could be used against MD5, with somewhat lower performance.
sections.plainLanguage: To know how long a password must be, you first guess how fast a burglar can try combinations. A burglar with a million helpers tries a lot more than one burglar alone.

sections.title: Key Lifetime and Entropy
sections.content:
Operational experience suggests keys for this option may live for months. The RFC wants a key length where guessing takes a small multiple of the key-change interval. These keys only provide authentication, not confidentiality, so an attacker learning an old key after a key change is not considered a threat.

Assuming a 90 day change interval and an attack rate of 1.0e13 MD5 operations per second, the minimum entropy is about 68 bits, rounded up to at least 80 bits (10 bytes). Allowing for hardware attacks with a large budget raises that to around 83 bits (11 bytes), which the RFC rounds to 12 bytes.

Human-language keys are weak. English has about 1.3 bits of entropy per character, so a 61 byte phrase would be needed for 80 bits and 73 bytes for 96 bits. The RFC prefers a random key of 96 bits or more, generated as described in RFC 1750.
sections.plainLanguage: A password made of normal words is easier to guess than one made of random letters. So the memo says to use random keys, and to make them long enough.

sections.title: Key Length and Implementation Advice
sections.content:
The shortest packet an attacker would use has 40 bytes of IP and TCP header. That leaves 24 bytes of the 64-byte MD5 block that can hold key material without extra cost to routers, while making the attacker's job much harder. The RFC says to pick the largest practical key length smaller than 25 bytes, but at least 12 bytes. Longer keys may spill into a second MD5 block for short BGP packets, which it does not see as a significant burden.

Some implementations accept only ASCII keys of 8 bytes or less. Word-like keys carry at most 12 bits of entropy, so a dictionary attack is quick. Such implementations SHOULD let users enter a binary key, for example by treating an ASCII key starting with 0x as hexadecimal. Implementations SHOULD NOT limit key length unnecessarily and SHOULD allow at least 16 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: If a lock only accepts tiny keys, thieves can try them all. Let people use long random keys instead.

sections.title: Sharing and Handling Keys
sections.content:
In practice these keys are often shared among many systems. The more systems and people handle a key, the likelier it is to leak. Anyone holding the key can forge packets that appear to come from any other holder, so the safest practice is to use a key between exactly two parties. Current implementations may make that hard. Shorter key lifetimes can partly offset wide sharing.

Keys are sensitive. When they are sent electronically, including when configuring routers, secure handling techniques MUST be used, and protocols such as S/MIME, TLS or SSH SHOULD be used where appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: A secret stops being secret when lots of people know it. Share each key with only the one friend who needs it, and pass it along safely.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The whole document is about security requirements for the keying material used with RFC 2385. The RFC states that it creates no new security exposures.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo only gives advice for keeping the secret safe, so it does not add any new dangers.
